title: A Typewriter for the Orchard
premise: In 1934, on a storm-battered stretch of the Oregon coast, Wren Sandoval keeps the Point Alder lighthouse and keeps her grief locked away, convinced history is something that happens to other people. When a half-drowned stranger named Elias Vane washes ashore carrying letters in the handwriting of Senator August Hale—a man publicly dead for two years—Wren realizes the 'corpse' has been alive, hiding, and writing testimony that could topple the men who faked his death to seize a timber empire. Elias needs the letters carried south past three checkpoints before the senator's enemies burn the coast clean of witnesses; Wren, who once lost everything by staying silent, agrees to carry them herself. At the final checkpoint Wren is caught and must choose between burning the evidence to save her life or surrendering it at the cost of her freedom—until Elias, presumed drowned again, arrives to take her place, and the two of them deliver the truth together, finding in each other not an escape from duty but a new one worth keeping.
about_author: Coral Nystrom spent a decade restoring coastal lighthouses along the Pacific Northwest before turning to fiction full-time, drawing her settings from fog-soaked winters and the oral histories of keeper families. She writes in longhand at a 1948 typewriter she claims was salvaged from a shipwreck, though she refuses to say which one.

chapters.title: The Light That Answers No One
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A routine winter night establishes her isolation: she winds the clockwork, logs the weather, and speaks aloud to no one. A letter from her late husband's sister urges her to sell the light and move inland. Emotional beat: grief worn smooth into habit, and the quiet terror of a life with nothing left to lose.

chapters.title: What the Sea Gives Back
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. After a three-day storm, Wren finds a man half-buried in kelp below the north bluff—alive, clutching an oilskin packet. She drags him to the keeper's cottage against her own instinct for solitude. Emotional beat: reluctant compassion overriding self-protection; the first crack in her invisibility.

chapters.title: A Handwriting Like a Ghost
chapters.summary: Elias's POV, feverish and fragmented. He wakes disoriented, hides the packet under floorboards, and studies Wren, unsure if she can be trusted. He recognizes her name from shipping manifests tied to the conspiracy. Emotional beat: paranoia sharpened by weakness; trust as a calculated risk rather than a feeling.

chapters.title: The Dead Man Writes Letters
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Tending Elias's fever, she glimpses the letters: unmistakable loops she'd know anywhere, because August Hale taught her sister penmanship years ago—and Hale has been dead since the ferry sinking of 1932. Emotional beat: vertigo as the fixed past comes loose; history stepping through her own door.

chapters.title: Terms of a Drowning Man
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Elias recovers enough to bargain: he'll tell Wren everything if she helps him reach Coos Bay within eleven days, before the syndicate's men finish sweeping the coast. Wren refuses, then reads the last letter—an account of who ordered the ferry sunk. Emotional beat: fury replacing numbness; duty redefined.

chapters.title: Inventory of a Small Life
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. She prepares to leave the light unattended for the first time in six years, cataloging what she owns and what she owes. A supply boat arrives early; its captain, Marta Reyes, notices the stranger and offers silence—for now. Emotional beat: the strange liberation of packing up a life you'd already abandoned.

chapters.title: Checkpoint One: The Toll Bridge
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Disguised as a fish buyer's clerk, Elias passes the first checkpoint while Wren watches from the truck, learning how fear moves through ordinary faces. A guard mentions a reward notice with Elias's description. Emotional beat: the intoxicating and corrupting taste of deception done well.

chapters.title: Letters We Never Sent
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Night in a boarding house; Elias reads her one letter per hour, building the case piece by piece—the timber syndicate, the bought coroner, the ferry. Wren confesses she stayed silent when her brother-in-law's logging accident was ruled his own fault. Emotional beat: intimacy forged through shared complicity.

chapters.title: The Man Who Owns the Rain
chapters.summary: Marta's POV (interlude). Supply captain Marta Reyes reports the stranger's presence to Deputy Corben—then lies about which direction they went, torn between the syndicate's money and a debt she owes Wren's late husband. Emotional beat: corruption shown from inside, as a series of small survivable choices.

chapters.title: Checkpoint Two: The Mill Town
chapters.summary: Dual POV. In Halloway Mill, the second checkpoint, they discover the town is company-owned down to the church hymnals. A millworker recognizes Hale's handwriting from old pay ledgers and must decide whether to raise the alarm. Emotional beat: power revealed not as violence but as ownership of every exit.

chapters.title: What Belonging Costs
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Sheltered overnight by the millworker's family, Wren feels the pull of community she exiled herself from—and sees what obedience has cost them. Elias argues they should split up; Wren refuses. Their first real argument becomes their first honest conversation. Emotional beat: belonging offered and feared in equal measure.

chapters.title: The Ferry Sinking, Retold
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias finally tells his whole story: he was Hale's secretary, smuggled off the ferry before it was scuttled, and has spent two years moving the letters town to town while everyone who helped him was bought or buried. Emotional beat: survivor's guilt laid bare; love beginning to look like a liability he can't afford.

chapters.title: Deputy Corben's Ledger
chapters.summary: Corben's POV (interlude). The deputy closes in, cross-referencing Marta's half-lie with a telegraph from Halloway. He is not a monster but a tired man paying a mortgage with small betrayals. Emotional beat: the banality of enforcement; evil as paperwork.

chapters.title: Eleven Miles of Bad Road
chapters.summary: Dual POV. A washed-out road forces them to travel on foot through logged-off hills, pursued. Elias takes a fall protecting the packet; Wren carries both him and the letters. They admit, without saying it, that this is no longer about the mission. Emotional beat: tenderness under pressure; love arriving sideways.

chapters.title: Checkpoint Three: The River Ferry
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The final crossing is guarded by Corben himself. They hide the letters in plain sight—in the binding of Wren's husband's logbooks—and Wren walks aboard alone as bait while Elias circles downstream. Emotional beat: courage as arithmetic; she counts what she's willing to lose and finds the number smaller than her fear.

chapters.title: The Reward Notice
chapters.summary: Corben's POV. On the ferry, Corben questions Wren and nearly lets her pass—until he spots the logbook bindings and understands. He detains her quietly, offering a deal: the letters for her freedom and his promotion. Emotional beat: temptation delivered kindly, which makes it heavier.

chapters.title: Burn It or Be Burned
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Locked in the ferry office, Wren weighs Corben's offer against everything the letters contain. She begins feeding pages toward the stove—not surrendering, but forcing Corben to choose between losing the evidence entirely or letting her walk. Emotional beat: the climax of agency; power reclaimed by someone who was taught to be invisible.

chapters.title: The Man from the Water Again
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias reaches the ferry, creates a diversion by letting himself be recognized, and trades his capture for Wren's release. Corben, holding Elias and half a burned archive, realizes the story will now come out with or without him—and chooses, for once, the side that lets him sleep. Emotional beat: sacrifice answered; the plot's machinery breaking open.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Dual POV. In a federal hearing room in Portland, the surviving letters are read aloud. Hale himself appears, alive and ruined, to confirm them. The syndicate's men scatter like startled birds. Emotional beat: vindication rendered quiet and procedural—history happening to them at last, in their favor.

chapters.title: Aftermath of Weather
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Weeks later, Wren returns to Point Alder to find the light dark and the lens salt-fogged. She cleans it, relights it, and decides—not for duty, but because she chooses it—that she will keep it. Marta brings news that Corben testified willingly. Emotional beat: home rechosen rather than endured.

chapters.title: A Typewriter for the Orchard
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias, cleared of his false death, buys back Hale's old typewriter at auction and brings it to the lighthouse, intending to write the full account. He asks, awkwardly, whether there is room in her orbit for a second keeper. Emotional beat: love against duty resolved—they choose each other without abandoning what they owe.

chapters.title: The Logbook, Continued
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, epilogue. One year later: the great storms return, and this time the light holds. Wren enters a new line in the logbook beside Elias's sleeping form upstairs—weather fair, lamp burning, all hands accounted for. Emotional beat: peace earned, not granted; the record finally telling the truth.
